Classical TO-based cloaks require anisotropic, highly inhomogeneous, and dispersive materials with parameters ranging from near zero to infinity.
Ideal invisibility cloaks require material parameters that tend to infinity at the inner boundary and unity at the outer boundary.
Metamaterials used in TO cloaks are narrowband, dispersive, and sensitive to polarization and incident angle.
The proposed design uses wideband, realistic materials that can be fabricated in the laboratory.
The cloak thickness in classical TO designs is comparable to the wavelength, which is undesirable for stealth applications.
The transformation optics algorithm is based on the invariance of Maxwell's equations under coordinate transformations.
The Jacobian matrix of the coordinate transformation relates permittivity and permeability tensors between physical and virtual domains.
The paper proposes discretizing the cloak region into radial cells with matched mesh sizes in physical and virtual domains to ensure smooth transitions.
The scale factor γ between physical and virtual domains must tend to zero for perfect invisibility, causing extreme material parameter requirements.
Thin TO cloaks show deteriorated performance when discretized into a few layers compared to ideal continuous parameter cloaks.
The alternative approach focuses on designing multilayer radar absorbing materials (RAMs) as planar absorbers for arbitrary shapes.
The designed absorbers achieve reflection levels below -10 dB over wide frequency bands (e.g., 2 to 18 GHz).
The proposed absorbing blankets are relatively insensitive to polarization and incident angle variations.
Graphene materials and embedded frequency selective surfaces can enhance absorber performance and bandwidth.
The integral form of Maxwell's equations is used to derive material parameters for arbitrary geometries beyond simple scaling.
The cloak region must have finite thickness to avoid discontinuities and fabrication issues.
The proposed method circumvents problems of narrow bandwidth and sensitivity inherent in TO-based cloaks.
Test cases demonstrate the application of the modified transformation electromagnetics design methodology.
Classical TO cloaks require metamaterials with parameters that are difficult or impossible to realize practically.
The paper emphasizes the practical realizability of the proposed cloak and absorber designs.
